title: Architecture
lead: Marble Lantern is one code base with three ways to run: a static site where every engine runs in your browser, a Spring Boot server that adds engines on the server, and command-line jobs that train the neural network. This page shows where each part runs, how one engine move travels, and where to find the code.
toc.build: From Java and C++ to the browser
sec.overview.title: One code base, three ways to run
sec.overview.p1: Marble Lantern plays Sternhalma (Chinese Checkers) for two players. The game is the workload, not the goal: the project shows Java on the GPU with {term:tornadovm|TornadoVM} and Java in the browser with {term:teavm|TeaVM}. The rules, the classical search and the {term:neural-network|neural network} are written in Java 25 and split into Gradle modules. A C++ port of the rules, the search and the network lives in `cpp/`. One React user interface in `web/src/` serves every way of running.
sec.overview.p2: The code runs in three places. The offline site is a set of static files: every {term:engine} runs in a {term:web-worker|Web Worker} inside your browser, and no server code runs. The online mode is a Spring Boot jar that serves the same React code and adds engines on the server. The training jobs are command-line JVM processes that produce the networks. Their output stays on the training machine; only a packed copy of a network enters the repository.
sec.overview.p3: The engines come in two kinds. The classical engine uses {term:alpha-beta|alpha-beta search} plus a {term:race-table|race table} for the end of the game, and it is the default in the browser. The network engines use {term:mcts|Monte Carlo Tree Search} guided by the neural network. {sec:classical/alpha-beta|Topic 2} explains the classical engine, {sec:inference/mcts|topic 3} the network engines.
sec.modules.title: Modules and directories
sec.modules.p1: The Java code is split into ten Gradle modules, listed in {src:settings.gradle.kts}. At the bottom sits `engine`: the board of {n:121} cells, the rules and the move generation, in plain Java with no dependencies. On top of it, `tablebase` builds and reads the race tables, `nn` holds the network and its CPU trainer, `nn-tornado` the GPU kernels, and `search` the players: alpha-beta, MCTS and the arena that plays matches between them. `selfplay` drives training and uses all of these.
sec.modules.p2: Three small modules exist only for the browser. `teavm-web` is a facade over the classical engine that TeaVM compiles into {term:wasm|WebAssembly} and JavaScript. `teavm-net` compiles the Java MCTS without the {term:forward-pass|forward pass}; the forward pass runs in C++ or on the GPU instead. `teavm-nn-bench` measured the Java network in the browser at 126 to 163 positions per second (SMALL network, one position per call, Apple M3 Max), and that result is why C++ computes the browser's forward pass. The tenth module, `app`, is the online server.
sec.modules.p3: Some top-level directories are not Gradle modules: `cpp/` holds the C++ port and its browser builds, `web/` the React app, `scripts/` one script per {term:devenv-task|devenv task}, and `docs/` the design documents. The tasks themselves are defined in {src:devenv.nix}. Three directories are git-ignored and exist only on a developer's machine: `data/` with the training runs, `cloud-results/` and `tornado-sdk/`. In the figure, you can open the tree and see which module depends on which.
sec.offline.title: Offline: everything in the browser
sec.offline.p1: In the offline site, the game never leaves your browser. The page runs on the main thread: the board, the game controller with the move history ({src:web/src/game/game.ts}) and the engine session ({src:web/src/app/session.ts}). Each engine runs in its own {term:web-worker|Web Worker}, a background thread with its own event loop. The worker sees none of the page's objects and talks to the page only through {term:post-message|postMessage}. The main thread never runs a search, so the board stays responsive while the engine thinks.
sec.offline.p2: One engine move is one request and one reply. The worker client ({src:web/src/engines/client.ts}) sends a `choose` request with an id and the whole move history as a `number[]`; each move is packed as `from | (to << 8)`. The worker replays the history, searches, and sends exactly one reply with the same id: the move, its score, the search depth and the number of positions searched. The message types are defined in {src:web/src/engines/protocol.ts}.
sec.offline.p3: Nothing can stop a search once it runs. When you undo a move while the engine is thinking, the client terminates the worker and starts a new one. The race table stays in the page's memory, so the restart downloads nothing. The {term:service-worker|service worker} ({src:web/src/pwa/sw.ts}) stores the page, the default engine and the race table when it installs (about {n:4.7} MB), and other engines and the models the first time they load. This makes the site a {term:pwa|PWA} that works offline.
sec.build.title: From Java and C++ to the browser
sec.build.p1: Java reaches the browser through {term:teavm|TeaVM}, an ahead-of-time compiler from JVM bytecode to JavaScript and WebAssembly. TeaVM 0.16.0 compiles the facade {src:teavm-web/src/main/java/sternhalma/web/Web.java} into {term:wasm-gc|Wasm GC}, WebAssembly with garbage collection. The result is the default engine `java-wasmgc`: about {n:610} kB, {n:210} kB with gzip. The same code compiled to plain JavaScript is the engine `java-js`. The script {src:scripts/web/build-teavm.zsh} runs both builds.
sec.build.p2: C++ reaches the browser through {term:emscripten|Emscripten}. The script {src:scripts/web/build-wasm.zsh} builds the classical engine `cpp-wasm` from the C API in {src:cpp/src/wasm/wasm_api.cpp}: about {n:330} kB, {n:120} kB with gzip, for browsers without Wasm GC. It also builds three variants of the C++ forward pass for the network engines. At start, the page picks the first engine that works, in the order `java-wasmgc`, `cpp-wasm`, `java-js` ({src:web/src/engines/registry.ts}).
sec.build.p3: Two kinds of data ship with the engines. {src:scripts/offline/pack-tables.py} compresses the race table `rows2.bin` with gzip to about {n:2.5} MB; the page checks its length and SHA-256 after the download ({src:web/src/engines/tables.ts}). {src:scripts/models/pack-model.py} packs each network as a {term:safetensors} file with {term:f32-f16|F16} weights and gzip, about {n:115} kB, and verifies it again when the build copies it into the site. Last, {src:scripts/web/build.zsh} runs Vite and fails if a bundled file contains the server path `connect/`.
sec.online.title: Online: engines on a server
sec.online.p1: The online mode packs the same React code into a Spring Boot jar with {term:hilla|Hilla}. A compile-time constant `__ONLINE__` is `true` only in this build ({src:app/vite.config.ts}), so the static build contains no server client at all. The classical browser engines still run in Web Workers. A server adapter ({src:web/src/engines/server/client.ts}) adds engines on the server: the browser's classical player, the strongest classical player with the large race table `rows1.bin` when the server has it, and a network player when a network file is configured.
sec.online.p2: A server move is one HTTP call: `POST /connect/GameEndpoint/choose` with the engine id, the move history as `int[]` and a node budget. {src:app/src/main/java/sternhalma/app/GameEndpoint.java} hands the call to {src:app/src/main/java/sternhalma/app/Engines.java}, which checks the budget (1 to {n:5000000}), replays the history and creates a fresh player for every call. The server is stateless: nothing carries over between calls, not even the {term:transposition-table|transposition table}. The reply is a `ServerChoice` record as JSON.
sec.online.p3: `Engines` limits how many searches run at once with a fair `Semaphore` that has one permit per `availableProcessors()`. A request waits at most 30 seconds for a permit and otherwise answers that the server is busy. The network player gets one {term:simulation} per 100 {term:node|nodes} of the budget and computes its {term:forward-pass|forward pass} with the {term:vector-api|Vector API} on the CPU or with TornadoVM on the GPU. That network object is not thread-safe, so a `synchronized` block lets one search use it at a time.
sec.training.title: Training jobs
sec.training.p1: Training does not run in the web app. Each step is a JVM process started from the command line, for example {src:scripts/loop.sh}, which runs {src:selfplay/src/main/java/sternhalma/selfplay/Loop.java}. One generation of the loop has four phases. The best network plays games against itself ({term:self-play}), and a candidate network trains on those games. A {term:gate} match against the best network decides whether the candidate replaces it, and the decision is written to disk. {sec:training/loop|Topic 4} explains each phase.
sec.training.p2: Everything a run writes lands in the git-ignored directory `data/<run>/`: sample files, {term:checkpoint|checkpoints}, the candidate network and a `decision.json` per generation. A job derives its phase from these files, so even a run stopped with `kill -9` continues where it stopped. The project made seven {term:loop-run|loop runs}, training runs of the loop with their own settings, numbered 1 to 7. With TornadoVM on the GPU, one generation of loop run 1 trained in {n:41.8} seconds instead of {n:22.9} minutes on the CPU. All training ran on one Apple M3 Max.
sec.training.p3: Only a chosen network leaves `data/`. {src:scripts/models/pack-model.py} converts its weights to {term:f32-f16|F16}, compresses them with gzip and writes them to `web/models/`, listed in {src:web/models/models.json}. The web build copies them into the site. The browser ships two such networks: a two-player expert from generation 13 of loop run 3, and a shared network for all four variants, two or three players with the neighbour jump or the long hop.
sec.threads.title: Threads, workers and promises
sec.threads.p1: A {term:web-worker|Web Worker} is the closest thing the browser has to a thread, with one difference that matters: it shares no objects with the page. Data cross over only inside messages, as copies or as transferred byte buffers. Picture a thread that owns its heap and talks to the rest of the program only through a queue. This is why each worker loads its own copy of the engine, and why the race table travels to the worker once, inside the `init` request.
sec.threads.p2: On the page, every engine method returns a `Promise`, the JavaScript counterpart of a `CompletableFuture`. The worker client keeps a map from request id to the open promise and completes the promise when the reply with that id arrives. No message can stop a search that is already running, so cancelling means terminating the worker, as {sec:architecture/offline|the offline section} describes.
sec.threads.p3: Training uses real Java threads, including virtual threads. During self-play on the GPU, hundreds of games run as virtual threads and hand their positions to one `PooledEvaluator` ({src:nn/src/main/java/sternhalma/nn/PooledEvaluator.java}). Its single device thread collects the positions into batches for the GPU, because the TornadoVM network is not thread-safe. Platform threads with permits reached only a third of that throughput ({src:selfplay/src/main/java/sternhalma/selfplay/LoopGamesJob.java}). Next, {sec:classical/board|topic 2} shows what the classical engine does inside its worker.
read.24.note: MDN reference for the browser GPU API that the `net-webgpu` engine uses for its forward pass.
read.25.note: Introduction to WebAssembly, the binary format that both browser engines are compiled to.
read.26.note: The compiler that turns the Java engine into WebAssembly and JavaScript for the browser.
read.27.note: The runtime that compiles Java methods into GPU kernels for training and the server's network player.
fig.offline.title: Offline: every engine in a Web Worker
fig.offline.desc: Box diagram of the offline site. The main thread holds the page, board, game URL, game controller, engine session, worker client, table loader and model list. Web Workers run the Java engine, the C++ engine and the net engine with its CPU or GPU forward pass. A service worker caches the files of the static host.
fig.offline.caption: Solid arrows carry data; dashed arrows start or trigger another part. Step through one engine move, or switch on the undo to see how a running search is cancelled. Select a box for its details and source files.
fig.offline.node.page.label: Browser page (React)
fig.offline.node.page.detail: The React app on the main thread. It draws the screens and passes your clicks to the game controller. It never runs a search, so the page stays responsive while an engine thinks.
fig.offline.node.board.label: Board (SVG)
fig.offline.node.board.detail: Draws the {n:121} cells as SVG and animates each move. The cell positions come from a generated geometry file.
fig.offline.node.gameUrl.label: Game URL
fig.offline.node.gameUrl.detail: Stores the whole game in the address fragment `#g=…`, so a link or a reload restores it. A move takes {n:14} bits, {n:7} for the start cell and {n:7} for the target cell; a game of {n:100} plies, single moves of one side, needs {n:1400} bits, written as {n:234} base64 characters.
fig.offline.node.controller.label: Game controller
fig.offline.node.controller.detail: `GameController` keeps the move history, knows the side to move and handles undo. When the engine is to move, it asks the engine session for a move.
fig.offline.node.session.label: Engine session
fig.offline.node.session.detail: `EngineSession` knows which engine plays, loads it and switches engines. At start it takes the first engine that works, in the order `java-wasmgc`, `cpp-wasm`, `java-js`.
fig.offline.node.workerClient.label: Worker client
fig.offline.node.workerClient.detail: `WorkerEngine` wraps a worker as an engine. It sends each request with an id and completes the matching `Promise` when the reply with that id arrives. To cancel a search, it terminates the worker.
fig.offline.node.tableLoader.label: Table loader
fig.offline.node.tableLoader.detail: Downloads `rows2.bin.gz` (about {n:2.5} MB), unpacks it with `DecompressionStream` and checks its length and SHA-256. It hands the bytes to the worker in the `init` request.
fig.offline.node.javaEngine.label: Java engine (Wasm GC or JS)
fig.offline.node.javaEngine.detail: The classical engine: Java compiled by TeaVM. The default build `java-wasmgc` has about {n:610} kB, {n:210} kB with gzip; `java-js` is the same code as plain JavaScript. It plays `BROWSER_SPEC`, alpha-beta search plus the race table.
fig.offline.node.cppEngine.label: C++ engine
fig.offline.node.cppEngine.detail: The C++ port of the classical engine, compiled by Emscripten, for browsers without Wasm GC: about {n:330} kB, {n:120} kB with gzip. Golden files check that it plays like the Java engine.
fig.offline.node.netMcts.label: Net engine: MCTS
fig.offline.node.netMcts.detail: The Java MCTS, compiled by TeaVM without a forward pass. The TypeScript side drives it: it takes a batch of positions from the search, has the backend evaluate them and hands the results back, until the search is done.
fig.offline.node.netCpu.label: Net engine: CPU forward pass
fig.offline.node.netCpu.detail: Computes the network in C++ compiled to WebAssembly. On an Apple M3 Max at batch 1 it evaluates about {n:3100} positions per second with 128-bit SIMD (`simd`) or {n:4000} with relaxed SIMD (`relaxed`), a newer WebAssembly extension.
fig.offline.node.netGpu.label: Net engine: GPU forward pass
fig.offline.node.netGpu.detail: Computes the network in WGSL shaders through WebGPU. On an Apple M3 Max it takes about {n:0.5} ms at batch 1 and reaches up to about {n:60000} positions per second at batch 16.
fig.offline.node.models.label: Models
fig.offline.node.models.detail: `models.json` lists the shipped networks. A network file is F16 safetensors with gzip: about {n:115} kB each for the expert and for the shared model. The net worker checks its SHA-256 and widens the weights to F32.
fig.offline.node.raceTable.label: Race table file
fig.offline.node.raceTable.detail: The race table `rows2.bin`: for each placement of {n:10} pieces near the goal, the exact number of moves to fill the goal. The build compresses it with gzip to about {n:2.5} MB.
fig.offline.node.serviceWorker.label: Service worker
fig.offline.node.serviceWorker.detail: Caches the site for offline use. At install it stores the page, the default engine and the race table, about {n:4.7} MB. Other engines and the models enter the cache the first time they load.
fig.offline.idle: Step forward to follow one engine move from your click to the animated reply.
fig.offline.step.1: You click a target cell. The page hands the move to `GameController`, which adds it to the history and sees that the engine is to move.
fig.offline.step.2: `GameController` asks the engine session for a move. The session passes the request to `WorkerEngine`, the client of the current engine's worker.
fig.offline.step.3: `WorkerEngine.choose` sends a `choose` request with an id and the whole history as `number[]` through `postMessage`. Each move is packed as `from | (to << 8)`.
fig.offline.step.4: The worker replays the history and searches. The main thread keeps running, so the board stays responsive.
fig.offline.step.5: The worker sends one `ChooseResult` with the same id: the move, its score, the depth and the number of nodes. `WorkerEngine` completes the open `Promise`.
fig.offline.step.6: `GameController` adds the engine's move to the history, and the board animates it.
fig.offline.cancel.step.1: You undo a move while the worker still searches. Nothing can stop a running search, so `WorkerEngine` terminates the worker.
fig.offline.cancel.step.2: `WorkerEngine` starts a new worker. The page still holds the table bytes, so the restart downloads nothing.
fig.offline.cancel.step.3: The new worker receives the table in its `init` request and waits for the next request. The undone move is gone from the history.
fig.online.title: Online: engines on the server
fig.online.desc: Box diagram of the online mode. In the browser: the page, the browser engines in Web Workers, the server adapter and the generated Hilla client. On the Spring Boot server: GameEndpoint, the engine service with its semaphore, the alpha-beta players with the race tables rows2 and rows1, and the network player with a CPU or GPU forward pass.
fig.online.caption: One server move is one HTTP call, and the server keeps nothing between calls. The slider only redraws the permits for the chosen number of requests: it shows the rule in the code, not a measurement.
fig.online.node.page.label: Browser page (same React code)
fig.online.node.page.detail: The Hilla entry `@index.tsx` mounts the same React app as the offline site. A compile-time constant `__ONLINE__` is `true` only in this build, so the static site contains no server client.
fig.online.node.browserEngines.label: Browser engines (as offline)
fig.online.node.browserEngines.detail: The classical browser engines still run in Web Workers. The jar serves their files and the race table `rows2` from its resources, so they work as in the offline site.
fig.online.node.serverAdapter.label: Server adapter
fig.online.node.serverAdapter.detail: `ServerEngineAdapter` makes a server engine look like any other engine. It rejects variants that the server does not play before it calls the server, and an `AbortSignal` cancels the HTTP request.
fig.online.node.hillaClient.label: Generated Hilla client
fig.online.node.hillaClient.detail: Hilla generates this TypeScript client from the Java endpoint, so every call is typed. It is a build product and not in Git. Each call is a `POST` with JSON and a CSRF token.
fig.online.node.endpoint.label: GameEndpoint
fig.online.node.endpoint.detail: `GameEndpoint` is the HTTP API with three methods: `engines()`, `legalMoves(history)` and `choose(engineId, history, nodes)`. It passes every call to the engine service.
fig.online.node.engines.label: Engine service and semaphore
fig.online.node.engines.detail: `Engines` checks the budget ({n:1} to {n:5000000} nodes), replays the history and takes a permit from a fair `Semaphore` with one permit per processor. It waits at most {n:30} seconds and otherwise answers that the server is busy.
fig.online.node.alphaBeta.label: Alpha-beta players
fig.online.node.alphaBeta.detail: A fresh `AlphaBetaPlayer` for every call: `BROWSER_SPEC` for the engine `browser`, `BEST_SPEC` for `best`. Nothing carries over between calls, not even the transposition table.
fig.online.node.raceTables.label: Race tables rows2 and rows1
fig.online.node.raceTables.detail: `rows2.bin` for every classical player, and the large `rows1.bin` of about {n:254} MB for the engine `best`. The server offers `best` only when it finds a valid `rows1.bin`. Both tables live in the JVM heap.
fig.online.node.networkPlayer.label: Network player
fig.online.node.networkPlayer.detail: MCTS with one simulation, one network-guided search path, per {n:100} nodes of the budget, at least one, at batch 1. It exists only when the server starts with a network file. A `synchronized` block lets one search at a time use the network.
fig.online.node.cpuForward.label: CPU forward pass
fig.online.node.cpuForward.detail: `VectorNetwork` computes the forward pass on the CPU with the Java Vector API. This is the default backend of the network player.
fig.online.node.gpuForward.label: GPU forward pass
fig.online.node.gpuForward.detail: `TornadoNetwork` computes the forward pass on the GPU. The server uses it when it starts with `sternhalma.app.backend=tornado` and the TornadoVM flags.
fig.online.node.jarBuild.label: Build of the jar
fig.online.node.jarBuild.detail: Gradle builds `app.jar` with Hilla's Vite build and copies the browser engines and the race table into it. It does not copy the models, so the browser's net engines probably cannot load a network in the online mode. Nobody has tested this.
fig.online.idle: Step forward to follow one server move from the page to the reply.
fig.online.step.1: The page asks the server adapter for a move. The adapter calls the generated Hilla client, an `async` function that returns a `Promise`.
fig.online.step.2: The client sends `POST /connect/GameEndpoint/choose` with the engine id, the history as `int[]` and the node budget.
fig.online.step.3: `Engines` checks that the budget lies between {n:1} and {n:5000000} nodes and replays the history from the start position.
fig.online.step.4: `Engines` calls `Semaphore.tryAcquire` and waits up to {n:30} seconds for a permit. Without a permit, it answers that the server is busy.
fig.online.step.5: With a permit, `Engines` creates a fresh player for this call and lets it search. Then it releases the permit.
fig.online.step.6: The server returns a `ServerChoice` record as JSON: move, score, depth, nodes and time. The adapter completes the `Promise`, and the board plays the move.
fig.online.semaphore.title: Permits of the semaphore
fig.online.semaphore.note: The server has one permit per processor (`availableProcessors()`). A request beyond that waits up to {n:30} seconds for a free permit.
fig.pipeline.title: The training pipeline
fig.pipeline.desc: Box diagram of training. Classical teacher games and generation 0 give the first samples and the first network. Then the loop repeats: self-play with MCTS writes sample files, the replay buffer feeds a CPU or GPU trainer, the trainer writes checkpoints, and the gate decides about the candidate. A chosen network is packed for the browser.
fig.pipeline.caption: Everything a run writes stays in the git-ignored directory `data/<run>/`; only a packed network reaches `web/models/`. The switch shows the training time per generation measured in loop run 1.
fig.pipeline.node.teacherGames.label: Classical teacher games
fig.pipeline.node.teacherGames.detail: `BEST_SPEC`, the strongest alpha-beta player, plays itself. A second search scores every legal move at the root exactly at depth 2 or 3, and these scores become the policy targets of the first samples: the move probabilities that the network learns.
fig.pipeline.node.gen0.label: Generation 0
fig.pipeline.node.gen0.detail: Trains the first network from scratch on the teacher samples, by supervised learning. The loop starts from this network.
fig.pipeline.node.loop.label: Loop driver
fig.pipeline.node.loop.detail: `Loop` runs one generation after the other: self-play, training, gate, decision. It derives the current phase from the files in the run directory, so a stopped run continues where it stopped.
fig.pipeline.node.selfPlayGames.label: Self-play games (virtual threads)
fig.pipeline.node.selfPlayGames.detail: The best network plays itself with MCTS. The code default is {n:600} games per generation at {n:100} simulations per move; loop runs 2 to 4 used {n:2500} games at {n:200}. With a GPU, hundreds of games run at once as virtual threads.
fig.pipeline.node.mcts.label: MCTS
fig.pipeline.node.mcts.detail: One search per move. During the first {n:14} plies the move is drawn at random in proportion to the visit counts, that is how often the search tried each move; after that the most visited move is played. Noise at the root adds variety.
fig.pipeline.node.pooledEvaluator.label: Pooled evaluator (batches across games)
fig.pipeline.node.pooledEvaluator.detail: Collects positions from many games into one batch for the device. Its single device thread calls the network, because `TornadoNetwork` is not thread-safe. Two cohorts take turns: one fills a batch while the device computes the other.
fig.pipeline.node.sampleFiles.label: Sample files
fig.pipeline.node.sampleFiles.detail: Safetensors files under `gen-NNNN/samples/`. A sample holds the position, the legal moves with the visit shares of the search as the policy target, and the game result as the value target.
fig.pipeline.node.replayBuffer.label: Replay buffer
fig.pipeline.node.replayBuffer.detail: Keeps the samples of the last generations in memory, up to a fixed window, and drops the oldest whole generation first. It draws batches at random with a fixed seed, so a resumed run draws the same batches.
fig.pipeline.node.trainerCpu.label: Trainer, CPU
fig.pipeline.node.trainerCpu.detail: The reference trainer in plain Java. It trains the candidate in batches of {n:256} with AdamW, the optimiser that turns gradients into weight updates, starting from the weights of the best network. One generation of loop run 1 took {n:22.9} minutes.
fig.pipeline.node.trainerGpu.label: Trainer, GPU (TornadoVM)
fig.pipeline.node.trainerGpu.detail: The same training as TornadoVM kernels on the GPU, at {n:55} to {n:68} times the samples per second of the CPU trainer. A whole generation of loop run 1 gained less: {n:41.8} seconds instead of {n:22.9} minutes, about {n:33} times faster.
fig.pipeline.node.checkpoint.label: Checkpoints
fig.pipeline.node.checkpoint.detail: The trainer saves its state every {n:50} steps or {n:60} seconds, atomically, and keeps the last two. A resumed run continues bit for bit. The last step becomes `candidate.safetensors`.
fig.pipeline.node.gate.label: Gate
fig.pipeline.node.gate.detail: The candidate plays the best network, MCTS against MCTS: {n:100} pairs of games by default, {n:200} in loop runs 2 and 3. It is promoted only if `score − 1.28 · se > 0.5`. The result goes to `decision.json`.
fig.pipeline.node.runDirectory.label: Run directory
fig.pipeline.node.runDirectory.detail: `data/<run>/` is git-ignored and exists only on the training machine. It holds `run.json` and one `gen-NNNN/` directory per generation. The best network is the newest promoted candidate; there is no pointer file.
fig.pipeline.node.packer.label: Packing for the browser
fig.pipeline.node.packer.detail: `pack-model.py` converts a chosen candidate to F16, compresses it with gzip and writes it to `web/models/`. The web build copies it to `web/public/models/` and checks it again.
fig.pipeline.node.cloud.label: Cloud (tests only)
fig.pipeline.node.cloud.detail: AWS spot instances ran compatibility tests only: an AVX-512 CPU test and CUDA tests on a Tesla T4. All training ran on one Apple M3 Max.
fig.pipeline.file.runJson: Settings of the run, with a hash
fig.pipeline.file.strength: Ladder games of the best network
fig.pipeline.file.metrics: Progress log of the whole run
fig.pipeline.idle: Step forward to follow one generation of the loop.
fig.pipeline.step.1: Self-play: the best network plays itself with MCTS. With a GPU, the games run as virtual threads and share one pooled evaluator.
fig.pipeline.step.2: Write samples: each finished game becomes samples in `gen-NNNN/samples/`, with the position, the visit shares of the search and the game result.
fig.pipeline.step.3: Train: the replay buffer draws batches from the recent generations. The trainer starts from the best network, writes checkpoints and finally `candidate.safetensors`.
fig.pipeline.step.4: Gate: the candidate plays the best network. It must score more than 0.5 by at least 1.28 standard errors.
fig.pipeline.step.5: Decide: `decision.json` records promoted or rejected. A promoted candidate plays the next self-play; after a rejection, the old network plays on.

fig.tree.title: Directories and modules
fig.tree.desc: A graph of the ten Gradle modules. An arrow from one module to another means “depends on”. engine sits at the bottom and depends on no other module. When a row of a module is selected in the tree, the graph marks that module, the modules it depends on and the modules that use it.
fig.tree.caption: Click or tap a row to see what it is, where it runs and its link to GitHub. The arrow in front of a folder opens or closes it. For a Gradle module the details also list its dependencies, and on a wide screen the graph marks them. The filter mutes the rows that do not run in the chosen place. Entries tagged “not in Git” exist only on a developer's machine, not in a fresh clone.
